utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Registrar, would you please cite the case under review today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the case of the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic, also known as Jenki. Case number IT-94-2-R61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Prosecuting counsel, at this hearing which deals with the application of Rule 61, I'd like to reiterate that according to the wording on the basis of the decision, the Prosecutor was supposed to read the most relevant parts of the indictment. Now, since this -- such a reading, shall we say, is going to be done by the Chamber in the course of its presentation of the decision, do you think it's necessary for you to read out the relevant parts of the indictment? THE PROSECUTOR: Your Honour, if Your Honour pleases, no. I think it's appropriate that it be incorporated into the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, under those circumstances, we will then adjourn following the presentation of the decision. Now, before I read the decision to you, I would like to give you a brief introduction for the benefit of others following these proceedings, and not just those who are here now, to outline the decision. We are going to begin with an introduction. The Chamber is going to explain how Rule 61 works. It's a procedural matter but it has a scope that goes well beyond that, and that is something I would like to explain. Subsequently, the Tribunal will describe the crimes which the accused Dragan Nikolic is alleged to have committed. Thereafter, they will be legally characterised, and this is the very basis of Rule 61. It is the matter of confirming the initial indictment. Thereafter, via this decision, we will suggest to the Prosecutor that he consider certain steps which we thought might be relevant. Then with regard to the formalities which have been undertaken with the view to the original indictment, and for the -- to see to it that the Registrar did go to [indiscernible] to serve the original indictment, and then to finish, we will comment on the future of this case. So this is the decision of Trial Chamber I of the International Criminal Tribunal: Introduction. By a decision dated 16 May 1995, pursuant to Rule 61(A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Rules, Judge Odio-Benito ordered that the Prosecutor submit to this Trial Chamber the indictment against Dragan Nikolic alleged to have been, during 1992, the Commander of Susica camp located in the region of Vlasenica in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Pursuant to Rules 46 and 55, the same Judge had confirmed the indictment on 4 November 1994 and issued a warrant of arrest which, to this day, has not been executed. The Chamber had the material which was initially submitted to the confirming Judge, but it has also heard in the public hearing, during the week of 9 to 13 October 1995, a number of witnesses and alleged victims. The Chamber is now called on to determine the putative responsibility of Dragan Nikolic, that is, to determine if there are reasonable grounds for believing that he has committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment, and if so to issue an international warrant for his arrest. The execution of the arrest warrant relies upon States' obligation to cooperate and to render judicial assistance provided for by Article 29 of the Statute. In effect, all States in the International Community will be bound, if the warrant is issued, to cooperate in searching for and arresting the accused who would, in consequence, become an international fugitive. Moreover, should the Chamber consider that the failure to effect service of the indictment and to execute the original warrant of arrest is attributable to a State or, under the terms of the Rules, to a self-proclaimed entity, it may so certify and it may inform the Security Council through the offices of the President of the Tribunal. Before reviewing the crimes allegedly committed by the accused, both the facts and the legal description of those facts, it is appropriate to assess the scope of Rule 61 in the context of its first application. Recourse to Rule 61 means that the Tribunal, which does not have any direct enforcement powers, is not rendered ineffective in the face of the nonappearance of the accused and can proceed with the case despite this deficiency. The review by a panel of judges sitting in a public hearing of an indictment initially confirmed by a single judge reinforces both the rights of the accused and enhances the solemnity and gravity of the Judge's decision. The Rule 61 procedure, which is initiated by the Prosecutor, cannot be considered a trial in absentia. It does not culminate in a verdict, nor does it deprive the accused of the right to contest in person the charges brought against him before the Tribunal. The rights of alleged victims should not, however, be discounted altogether. Rule 61 will provide them with the opportunity to have their voices heard in a public hearing and to become part of history. We are now going to review the crimes which Dragan Nikolic allegedly committed. The crimes described hereunder were allegedly perpetrated during 1992 in Eastern Bosnia, in the municipality of Vlasenica and, for the most part, within the Susica camp, a former military installation converted by the Bosnian Serbs into a detention camp, and of which Dragan Nikolic is alleged to have been the commander. The detainees were held in one of the two main buildings within the camp called the hangar. Now, first the criminal acts. The Chamber now examines the evidence which has been tendered in support of the indictment in order to determine whether that evidence provides reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed any or all of the crimes charged in the indictment. The indictment against Dragan Nikolic consists of 24 counts. Each count relates to one set of facts for which the Prosecutor has proposed alternative legal descriptions. For the reasons discussed below, each count, with two exceptions, will here be presented under the most suitable description, that is, crimes against humanity. Murders first. A) The murders of Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. A number of witness statements, written and oral, of persons detained in Susica camp reported the murder of Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. Those testimonies indicate that one evening in June 1992, Dragan Nikolic and camp guards went towards the hangar and called out Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. The latter, shortly after having stepped from the hangar, was subjected to major physical assaults inflicted for more than 45 minutes by Dragan Nikolic and the guards. They were punched and kicked and struck with truncheons and rifle butts. Some prisoners witnessed some of the assaults as suffered, and others heard the victims cry out, scream, moan, and beg for an end to their torture. Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic were then brought back into the hangar. According to the testimony of prisoners who were there, their bodies were covered with bruises and their clothes were soiled and torn. Asim Zildzic had been beaten so violently that his face was unrecognisable and one eye had come out of its socket. He died shortly after having been brought back. Dragan Nikolic ordered his body to be taken away and two prisoners, Hasim and Alija Ferhatovic to bury him. Dragan Nikolic came into the hangar the next morning and approached Durmo Handzic. The latter was suffering intensely from the beating the night before, and Nikolic prohibited prisoners from helping him. Durmo Handzic thereupon begged Nikolic to kill him, to put an end to his suffering. Nikolic answered that a bullet was worth more than his life, that it would be wasted on him and that he should suffer before dying. Durmo Handzic died shortly afterwards. He was buried the same day by Hasim and Alija Ferhatovic. B) Murder of Mevludin Hatunic. Mevludin Hatunic, his wife, and daughter were turned in the Susica camp in early July 1992. Mevludin Hatunic reportedly offered his home to a Serb guard in return for his family's release. He was authorised to accompany the guard to his house for that purpose and then returned to the camp. This was between 3 and 7 July 1992. That same evening, Dragan Nikolic announced to the camp prisoners that after having handed over his home, Mevludin Hatunic had made a comment to the effect that he would be waiting for a chance to get even. Nikolic then hit Mevludin Hatunic. The following morning, Dragan Nikolic again beat him up until he lost consciousness. Dragan Nikolic returned that evening, saw that Mevludin Hatunic had regained consciousness and beat him savagely for the third time. Mevludin Hatunic died from his injuries. His body was put in a plastic bag by one of the Ferhatovic brothers and removed from the hangar. C) Murders of Rasid Ferhatbegovic, Dzevad Saric, Muharem Kolarevic, and Ibrahim Zekic. According to a number of witnesses, probably in the night from 23 to 24 June 1992, Rasid Ferhatbegovic, Dzevad Saric, Muharem Kolarevic, and Ibrahim Zekic were taken from the detainees' hangar by Goran Tesic and other guards. Some detainees saw Dragan Nikolic follow the prisoners out and heard his voice. Dzevad Saric and Muharem Kolarevic were the first to be taken out. The hangar doors were closed again immediately. For about 30 minutes, the detainees heard screams of pain. Thereafter they heard gunshots, following which Goran Tesic asked Hasim Ferhatovic to come out. The latter saw the bodies of Muharem Kolarevic and Dzevad Saric which seemed to have bullet wounds in the chest. Dragan Nikolic thereupon ordered the Ferhatovic brothers to put the bodies on a stretcher and take them behind the warehouse where they could not be seen from the camp entrance. They then came to where Nikolic, Tesic, a guard named Djuro and Dragan Nikolic's brother were sitting with others. Goran Tesic told them, "Hold on a minute. You're going to get another." Goran Tesic ordered Alija Ferhatovic to go and get Ibrahim Zekic. Goran Tesic had him sit down on a metal chair and questioned him. He then asked another guard to give him his weapon, and once he had it, he shot Ibrahim Zekic twice, who fell from the chair. Goran Tesic thereupon ordered the Ferhatovic brothers to take Ibrahim Zekic away. When they returned to where they had left the bodies of Muharem Kolarevic and Dzevad Saric, Muharem Kolarevic's body was no longer there. They brought this to Goran Tesic's attention. The prisoners who were in the hangar heard the guards yell, "Call the police. They're escaping." The police arrived some 15 minutes later and entered the hangar accompanied, according to some detainees, by Dragan Nikolic and Goran Tesic. Rasid Ferhatbegovic looked up. One of the police officers pointed at him and asked him if he was the one who had escaped. Tesic replied yes. Rasid Ferhatbegovic was taken outside and the prisoners then heard a gunshot. Towards 5.00 a.m., Dragan Nikolic came into the hangar and called Hasim and Alija Ferhatovic. They went over to the toilets where they found the body of Muharem Kolarevic. He was slumped over a barbed wire fence. Traces of blood led from where his body had been left the night before. Even though he seemed to be dead, Goran Tesic fired another bullet into the body. Hasim and Alija Ferhatovic carried the body to where they had left the other bodies the previous evening. There they found Rasid Ferhatbegovic with a bullet in the middle of the forehead. Hasim and Alija Ferhatovic and Redjo Cakisic buried the bodies of those prisoners on 24 June 1992. The murder of Ismet Dedic. Around 6 July 1992, Dragan Nikolic had Ismet Dedic come out of the detainees' hangar. He closed the door and the detainees thereafter heard Ismet Dedic scream. Shortly after, Dragan Nikolic opened the hangar door and ordered two detainees to drag Ismet Dedic inside. The latter was seriously wounded and died a little while later. His body was put in a plastic bag and carried away by other detainees. That concludes what is characterised as murders. Inhumane acts. First, inhumane acts committed against Galib Music. Dragan Nikolic committed serious physical assaults against Galib Music in Susica camp over a seven-day period. Dragan Nikolic allegedly kicked him and beat him with a metal bar. Galib Music was beaten unconscious each time. The beatings appeared to become more severe every day. Shortly before the last beating, Galib Music regained consciousness and asked for water. He was not given any water, food, or medical attention during the entire time he was tortured. Galib Music died as a result. B) Inhuman acts against Sead Ambeskovic [phoen]. Dragan Nikolic and other guards committed physical assaults against Sead Ambeskovic in Susica camp using axe handles, iron bars, wooden bats, and rifle butts. According to Sead Ambeskovic's testimony, as a result of the beatings, "The back of my head was cut, four teeth on the left side of my mouth were knocked out, and three ribs were broken." C) Inhumane acts committed against Redjo Cakisic. When he arrived in Susica camp, Redjo Cakisic was told by Nikolic and the camp guards, "Look how you ended up by voting for Alija Izetbegovic and the SDA party." According to his testimony at the hearing, Redjo Cakisic was called out by Nikolic one night. Nikolic told the two men waiting outside, "Here, I brought you something for dinner." The two men beat him in the back with rifle butts and kicked him in the stomach as Nikolic was leaving. D) Inhuman acts committed against Hasna Cakisic. On three occasions, the guards called out Hasna Cakisic for interrogation. According to the record, the 68-year-old victim was slapped and beaten on her hands with a truncheon to force her to reveal the whereabouts of her son. Dragan Nikolic participated in this ill-treatment. Generally speaking, in Susica camp, civilians were detained under inhumane conditions, especially as regards hygiene, health, safety, and nutrition. Included in the approximately 500 civilians were women, children, and elderly people. The detainees were crammed into a hangar with practically no ventilation and had to sleep on the concrete floor. They were given only one daily ration of food, and even that was usually spoiled. They were infrequently allowed to use the toilet outside and had to use a single bucket in the hangar for their bodily functions. No medical care was provided. Certain prisoners were specifically appointed to control the hangar. The detainees lived in constant fear for their lives, especially at night. I quote, "At night everybody waited for the day to come because that meant going out to work, not seeing what was happening. The torture and suffering were less severe, whereas the nights were nights of horror. Old people were not spared this inhuman treatment." As the witness described, "A 75- to 80-year-old woman, she wanted to go to the toilet but was not allowed to. Dragan Nikolic ordered her to be tied up, so they tied her hands and feet and she had to urinate the room we were in." In addition to the four victims mentioned above, the indictment alleges that Mevludin Hatunic, Ismet Dedic, and Fikret Cice Arnaut were victims of inhumane acts, Counts 3(6), 8(6), 11(3) [as interpreted]. As Nikolic is also charged with the murder of Hatunic and Dedic, the relevant acts are described under murders. As Nikolic is also charged with torturing Fikret Cice Arnaut, the relevant acts are described under torture. We will now go on to the paragraph on torture. Torture of Fikret Cice Arnaut. Fikret Cice Arnaut was allegedly assaulted by Nikolic on numerous occasions. Witnesses related how, on one occasion, Nikolic came into the hangar and while shouting to the women, "You are not here because of me but because of him. He wanted to rape my mother and now we will rape you." He forced Arnaut, Fikret Cice Arnaut, to put his hands behind his back and kneel on the floor, spreading his knees open. Dragan Nikolic kicked Fikret Cice Arnaut in the stomach and lower back. He forced him to tilt his head back and he put a bayonet into his mouth. Witnesses saw blood on Dragan Nikolic's bayonet. Later, Fikret Cice Arnaut was spitting and vomiting blood. He was heard begging, "Nikolic, don't beat me to death. Kill me with a bullet," to which Dragan Nikolic answered, "No. A bullet costs five German marks and you're not worth half a cigarette." Fikret Cice Arnaut was also taken outside and beaten by Dragan Nikolic who was wearing brass knuckles. According to one eyewitness, at one point, Fikret Cice Arnaut could no longer stand. He was covered with blood and his face was swollen. It appeared as though many of Arnaut's bones had been broken. Torture of Mubin Music. Mubin Music was mistreated while he was in Susica camp. While he was outside the hangar, Nikolic put a bayonet into his mouth, insulting and questioning him all the while. Torture of Suad Mahmutovic. Suad Mahmutovic was allegedly beaten repeated by Dragan Nikolic. Several witnesses, including the victim, asserted that during one beating, seven of his ribs were broken. Another time, Dragan Nikolic kicked him in the face with his boots and hitting him with a baton, gashing open his face. According to the witness, "One time in the hangar, Nikolic put a cocked pistol in my mouth and told me to admit my neighbour had a weapon. I feared for the safety of others and could not lie. He pulled the trigger. It was then that I realised the gun was not loaded." The Chamber notes that it appears that several other victims of inhumane acts or torture committed by Dragan Nikolic in Susica camp have not been identified as such in the indictment. Now we will proceed with the imprisonment of civilians. According to the written testimony as well as the oral testimony presented to the Chamber, a great number of people were detained at Susica camp during the period between 1st of June, 1992 and the 30th of September, 1992. The regular population of the camp is said to have been about 500. The majority of the detainees were men, but women and children are said to have also been part of that regular population. Over the entire period in question, 8.000 people in all are said to have been detained in Susica camp. All the witnesses who testified to having been detained at Susica camp emphasised that at the time of their arrest they had not been participating in a resistance movement against the authorities who had seized power in Vlasenica and who were responsible for the camp. It does not seem that such a movement could have taken shape in the Vlasenica region where the detainees were locals during the period in which the camp was operational. The arrests seem to have taken place only after the population had been totally disarmed. Thus, it would appear that the establishment of Susica camp was aimed at detaining a defenceless civilian population which was not organised into a resistance movement. Now we will proceed with the persecution on religious grounds. In the light of the relevant parts of the record, the imprisonment of civilians under particularly inhumane conditions might constitute an act of persecution since it appears to be motivated solely by a discriminatory intent based principally, if not exclusively, on the religious characterisation of the targeted population. The oral testimony at the hearing indicates that the camp population seemed to have been exclusively Muslim. Now we will talk about the appropriation of property and plunder. Many witnesses have provided evidence of a system of unlawful appropriation or plunder of property at Susica camp. The evidence is that on arrival at the camp, each detainee was forced to hand over items of private property, especially valuable items such as gold or jewelry. Dragan Nikolic is alleged to have personally supervised the confiscation of property while he was in a small building which he used for interrogations. There is also evidence that before women were deported from Susica camp, they had to sign a document stating that they were leaving the area voluntarily and that they were giving up their possessions. The Chamber considers that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the appropriations were not justified by military necessity and were carried out unlawfully and wantonly. The Chamber further considers that the acts described above could also be considered as characterising persecution on religious grounds and so be covered by Article 5 of the Statute. Unlawful transfer of civilians. Under the supervision and on the orders of the accused Dragan Nikolic, a large number of detainees were said to have been unlawfully transferred from Susica camp to Batkovic camp during the summer of 1992. Dragan Nikolic is said to have organised the transfers, calling out detainees from a list of names and telling them that they were to be exchanged for Serbian prisoners. In actual fact, the detainees were transferred to Batkovic camp. They were forced to travel by bus, with their heads down, their hands behind their heads. They were beaten and forced to sing patriotic Serbian songs. At Batkovic camp, conditions were similar to those at Susica camp, if not worse. As submitted by the Prosecutor, the Chamber considers that Dragan Nikolic may have committed grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, in particular, of the Fourth Convention, which comes under -- which come under the Tribunal's jurisdiction, pursuant to Article 2 of the Statute. The Chamber, however, also considers that the same set of facts could be characterised as deportation and accordingly come under Article 5 of the Statute. Crimes against humanity. We're now going to look into what type of responsibility arose out of Nikolic's position at the Susica camp. The relevant part of the record provides reasonable grounds for believing that Dragan Nikolic held the position of camp commander at Susica camp. The witnesses base their conclusions upon an analysis of the distribution of tasks within the camp. The guards were subjugated to Nikolic's order. Nothing apparently could be carried out without his assent. The witnesses also referred to declarations by Nikolic himself proclaiming his sovereign power within the camp. According to corroborated testimony, he would publicly state, "I am here. I am the commander, God, stick, and the law." The indictment and supporting material showed that Nikolic's responsibility for the crimes against identified persons could arise not only as a result of his direct involvement in committing such crimes, Article 7(1) of the Statute, the one who directly took responsibility, but also by his position of authority when the evidence does not suggest such direct involvement, which is the case for Counts 4, 5, 6, 7, and 18. This latter principle of individual responsibility for admission, that is, that he did not take all steps that he should have, long recognised under international criminal law, is reaffirmed by Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal which provides the fact that any of the acts referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the present Statute was committed by a subordinate does not relieve a superior of criminal responsibility if he knew or had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit such acts or had done so and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. However, with respect to the counts of the indictment concerning crimes against a group of persons, Counts 20 to 24, it should be noted that the reference to Article 7(3) is less pertinent. Dragan Nikolic's position of authority in the Susica camp makes him responsible not through his subordinates, but on his account where imprisonment, appropriation, deportation, persecution, and inhumane acts related to the very conditions of detention are concerned. The Chamber finished the review of all of the crimes of which Dragan Nikolic is suspected and now will move into the third part, the appraisal of the general context in which the alleged crimes are alleged to have been committed and will now say what it thinks the characterisation should be in priority. The Chamber has noted the alternative presentation in the indictment which the Prosecutor presented of the legal characterisation of the crimes. On the basis of relevant parts of the record, the Tribunal's jurisdiction may conceivably be founded on Articles 2 or 3 of the Statute. However, without prejudicing the appraisal of the Judges hearing the case, who one day, if Nikolic is arrested, will have to take the trial, feel that there are reasons to believe that the crimes are more suitably characterised as crimes against humanity, and the Chamber will now give its reasons for that. First it will look into the proof which will allow us to set the priority of those crimes which fall into the context of crimes against humanity, and we'll look at the context in which those crimes must be committed in order to be crimes against humanity. And then it will point out, through this definition, the various elements of the record that are the most relevant and that will be cited. First of all, the context in which crimes must be committed to be characterised as crimes against humanity. If I can remind you that first, Article 5 of the Statute reads: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons for the following crimes when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal, and directed against any civilian population: Murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, imprisonment, torture, rape, persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds, other inhumane acts." The definition specifies the type of crimes which, if committed under certain circumstances, constitute crimes against humanity and moreover describes those circumstances. The first circumstance referred to in the text is that of armed conflict. It is, in fact, common to Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Statute, dealt with alternatively or cumulatively in the indictment, which is why it will be addressed below. The Appeals Chamber thus confirmed the findings of the Trial Chamber and considered that by requiring demonstration of the existence of an armed conflict, the Statute had narrowed the customary concept of crimes against humanity, a decision of 2 October 1995, case number IT-94-1-A-72, paragraph 141. That concept, since the Nuremberg judgement, had taken on a certain autonomy as there was no longer any need to determine a link with a crime against peace or a war crime. The second circumstance, whereby crimes must be directed against any civilian population, is specific to crimes against humanity. Set forth in broad terms in the Statute, it apparently covers three distinct components according to the three prevailing opinions. First, the crimes must be directed at a civilian population specifically identified as a group by the perpetrators of those acts. Secondly, the crimes must be part of an organised and systematic approach; although they need not be related to a policy established at the level of the state in the conventional sense of the term, they cannot be the work of isolated individuals alone. Lastly, the crimes considered as a whole must be perpetrated on a broad scale and be very serious. Then having moved to this investigation of the first objective of the test, we'll now raise the question as to know whether Dragan Nikolic participated during 1992 in a systematic, serious, and widespread policy directed against a civilian population specifically identified as a group. The evidence produced by the Prosecutor tends to show that in the spring of 1992, in the Vlasenica region, there was an authoritarian takeover by the Serbs which seems to have been largely facilitated by the intervention of elements of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and in particular the Novi Sad Corps, which at that time was under the command of the government of Belgrade. The eyewitnesses generally confirmed the existence of a new authoritarian power structure at Vlasenica and were unanimous in stating that discriminatory measures were directed against them as early as March/April 1992. Some banking institutions imposed restrictions on the accounts of individuals of Muslim faith. Laissez-passer were issued in order to control movement both within and outside the city. A witness said at the hearing, "I never received a laissez-passer to leave the municipality of Vlasenica, but I was issued a laissez-passer to travel between my home and my land and my farm." Lastly, the population was required to hand in any and all weapons. The conclusion from all of the case material is that the civilian population subjected to the above-mentioned discrimination was identified by the perpetrators of the discriminatory measures principally by its religious characteristics. The testimony is consistent on this point. The Muslim population was specifically, if not exclusively, targeted. The initial discriminatory measures seem to have been followed by still more radical ones such as summary arrests, detentions, and torture at the police station, massive transfers of civilians to Susica and then to the Batkovic camp. On the basis of all the testimony, in September 1992, there remained only a few traces of the population of Muslim faith of the opstina of Vlasenica which, according to the 1991 census, the last census prior to the said events, amounted to 55.3 per cent of the total population. The implementation of that discriminatory policy, commonly referred to as ethnic cleansing, over the region of Vlasenica alone seems to have been some extensive that the Tribunal might be deemed competent under Article 5. However, the Chamber notes that the serious discriminatory acts do not seem to have been limited to the Vlasenica region. Camps like the one in Susica were set up in a large part of the territory under Serb control in Bosnia. This policy of ethnic cleansing covered other parts of Bosnia from the spring of 1992 on. According to the expert witness, the conduct of the spring 1992 attacks, including the manner in which the JNA and paramilitary groups deployed and treated the non-Serb population was similar throughout Bosnia. The deposition of this witness shows the extensiveness of the criminal acts which were committed, as well as the fact that they were organised at the highest level. According to the witness, the speed and high level of coordination that these attacks required made clear that they were centrally coordinated and planned. And the witness finished by saying, "In conjunction with Serbian political leaders and Serbian irregular units, the JNA conceived, planned, prepared, and implemented an armed campaign in Bosnia that involved a systematic use of terror to establish the borders of a new Yugoslavia." According to all the witnesses, Dragan Nikolic was the commander of the Susica camp at Vlasenica from the end of May 1992 to late September 1992. On that basis and in light of all the above, the Chamber considers that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he participated in such a policy and committed crimes against humanity pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute. Nonetheless, the Chamber has continued to review, in order to give the most complete answer to the request of the Prosecutor, and looking into the conditions for the applications of Article 2 and 3 of the Statute, that is, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and violation of the laws or customs of war respectively. Let us begin with the issue of the existence of an armed conflict and then the specific conditions for application. In certain cases, a condition for the Tribunal's competence ratio materi [phoen] is a state of armed conflict. Accordingly, this Chamber shall examine whether such a state of affairs prevailed at Vlasenica at the time that the crimes were committed. The Appeals Chamber of the Tribunal in the Tadic case said that, "An armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between States or protected armed violence between governmental authorities and organised groups or between such groups within a State." According to the deposition of Mr. James Gall [phoen], expert witness, the armed conflicts in the former Yugoslavia began in the summer of 1991 and continued out peaceful settlement to the present day. In this case, witnesses have provided testimony regarding the armed takeover of the town of Vlasenica both by the Bosnian Serbs and the JNA. Thus, the Chamber accordingly considers that the crimes of which Dragan Nikolic is accused were committed in armed conflict. Now we will look into the specific requirements for the application of Article 2 of the Statute having to do with serious violations of the provisions of the Geneva Convention. For it to be applied, the victims must be persons who are persons protected under the provisions of the relevant Geneva Convention. The Muslim population of Vlasenica was systematically disarmed, and it does not appear that there was any resistance movement in the region. The Chamber considers that all the detainees at Susica camp were civilians and therefore protected persons within the meaning of Article 4 of the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. The Appeals Chamber further stipulated in the said case of Tadic that the Tribunal has jurisdiction under Article 2 of the Statute only in the context of an international armed conflict. The relevant parts of the record tend to show that troops of the JNA from Novi Sad, under the command of the government in Belgrade, participated in the occupation of Vlasenica after Bosnia-Herzegovina had been recognised as an independent state. The evidence of the expert witness Mr. Gall suggests moreover that the armed conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia may be viewed in its entirety as one major armed conflict that reportedly began in the autumn of 1991, with its aim to establish a new state, and would have involved several states. The Chamber considers, on the basis of the foregoing, that the armed conflict was international in character and Article 2 may, therefore, be applicable. Now the Chamber will review the specific requirements for the application of Article 3 of the Statute. In its decision on the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in the Tadic case, the Appeals Chamber affirmed that the Tribunal is competent under Article 3 of the Statute to prosecute as violations of the laws or customs of war, and I quote, "All violations of international humanitarian law not falling under Article 2 or covered by Articles 4 or 5, more specifically, crimes against humanity and genocide, more specifically: 1, violations of The Hague Law on International Conflict; 2, infringements of provisions of the Geneva Conventions other than those classified as grave breaches by those conventions; 3, violations of Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and other customary rules on internal armed conflict; 4, violations of the agreements binding upon the parties to the conflict considered qua treaty law." The indictment against Nikolic contains 20 charges of violating the laws or customs of war under Article 3 of the Statute. All but one of those charges concerns violations of Article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions. In light of the Appeals Chamber with respect to that Article, and in light of our finding that the detainees at Susica camp were civilians and therefore persons taking no active part in the hostilities, the Chamber considers that Article 3 of the Statute may apply in this case. The only charge not coming under Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions concerns the prohibition on plunder of private property, but that is specifically mentioned in Article 3(e) of the Statute. After we have described all the acts that were allegedly committed, after we have legally analysed, now we would ask the Prosecutor to complete the indictment. Based on this review of the indictment, and in the light of all materials submitted by the Prosecutor, the Chamber would like to draw the Prosecutor's special attention to two points which it deems to be particularly important. Having regard to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it is the prerogative of the Prosecutor, not the Chamber, to amend the indictment according to Rule 50 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under these circumstances, the Chamber can only express a conclusion and invite the Prosecutor to amend the indictment accordingly should he share such conclusion. This concerns the rape and sexual assault and, on the other hand, ethnic cleansing and genocide. Let's first have a look into the rape and sexual assault. From multiple testimonies and victim and witness statements submitted by the Prosecutor to this Trial Chamber, it appears that women and girls were subjected to rape and other forms of sexual assault during their detention at Susica camp. Dragan Nikolic was allegedly directly involved in some of these rapes or sexual assaults. These allegations do not seem to concern isolated instances. The Trial Chamber feels that the Prosecutor may be well advised to review these statements carefully with a view to ascertaining whether to charge Dragan Nikolic with rape and other forms of sexual assault as a crime against humanity or as grave breaches or war crimes. Without prejudice to the appraisal of the Trial Judges, and in view of the special provisions on this subject contained in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Chamber would concur with the Prosecutor's proposition that rape and other forms of sexual assault inflicted on women in circumstances such as those described by the witnesses are acts of torture. After rape and sexual assault, the Chamber has deemed it extremely important to look into ethnic cleansing and genocide. It emerged on the basis of the evidence that the policy of discrimination implemented at Vlasenica, of which Dragan Nikolic's acts formed a part, was specifically aimed at cleansing the region of its Muslim population. In this instance, this policy of ethnic cleansing took the form of discriminatory acts of extreme seriousness which tend to show its genocidal character; for instance, the Chamber notes the statements by some witnesses which point, among other crimes, to mass murders being committed in the region. More specifically, the specific intent inherent to the crime of genocide may be deduced from the very gravity of those discriminatory acts. That intent, according to some of the eyewitnesses at the hearing, was expressly stated by the accused. Dragan Nikolic reportedly said, I quote, "You Muslims never existed," or "You will never exist. I will eradicate you. I will slit your throats. I will butcher you all." The Chamber considers that the Tribunal might possibly have jurisdiction in this case under Article 4 of the Statute. It would therefore invite the Prosecutor to pursue his investigations, if feasible and advisable, with a view to indicting Dragan Nikolic for complicity in genocide or acts of genocide. In order to respect the disposition of Rule 61, the Chamber has now to see whether everything was done in order to serve the indictment, and with regard to this, our decision is as follows: The Chamber notes the efforts by the Prosecutor to effect service of the original indictment and the subsequent warrants of arrest. On the 4th of November, 1994, the day the indictment against Dragan Nikolic was confirmed, two warrants for his arrest were issued; one addressed to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the other addressed to the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale, in accordance with Rules 2(A) and 55 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 7th of November, 1994, the Registrar of the Tribunal forwarded the warrant addressed to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the relevant authorities in Sarajevo. On the 15th of November, 1994, the Registrar received official notification that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was unable to execute the arrest warrant due to the fact that Dragan Nikolic, the accused, resides in the town of Vlasenica, which was stated to be "temporarily occupied territory controlled by aggressors." On the 17th of November, 1994, the warrant addressed to the Bosnian Serb authorities was physically handed by an official of the Tribunal to the members of the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale, including Mr. Koljevic, the declared Vice-President of the Bosnian Serb administration. On the 2nd of March, 1995, the Prosecutor sought to advertise the indictment in newspapers having wide circulation in the territory, as provided for in Rule 60. Accordingly, on the 13th of March, 1995, the Registrar forwarded to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina a request for publication. A similar request was also forwarded the same day to the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale. An article announcing an indictment against Dragan Nikolic was published in the newspaper Oslobodenje, the largest daily newspaper circulated in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 8th of April, 1995. In addition, the details of the indictment were broadcast repeatedly on the radio and television of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 7th of April, 1995. There has been no response from the Bosnian Serb administration concerning its willingness or ability to execute the warrant of arrest issued against Dragan Nikolic. At the end of this analysis, on the basis of the elements of the file, of the record, the Chamber takes the following disposition: For the foregoing reasons, and pursuant to Rule 61 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, pursuant to the confirmation of the indictment by Judge Odio-Benito, dated 4 November 1994, pursuant to the decision of 16 May 1995 by which the same Judge ordered the Prosecutor to submit the case to the Trial Chamber, and following the hearings of 9 to 13 October 1995 held at the seat of this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber unanimously determines that there are reasonable grounds for believing that Dragan Nikolic committed the offences with which he is charged in the indictment issued against him by the Prosecutor and dated 1 November 1994; confirms, therefore, this entire indictment comprised of 24 counts as described above; issues an international arrest warrant against Dragan Nikolic and states that such warrant shall be transmitted to all States; takes formal note of the efforts by the Prosecutor to effect service of the indictment and states that the failure to effect service is due wholly to the failure or refusal of the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale to cooperate; certifies this failure and invites the President of the Tribunal to notify the Security Council of the United Nations accordingly. Dated this 20th day of October, 1995, at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, in The Hague, the Netherlands. This session is closed.
